x.text:
It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like.

Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. 

This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.
x.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
x.textZh:
令人惊叹的是，我们已抵达这样一个临界点：AI 在训练模型方面比人类更高效，且这一转变迅速变得切实可行。前一刻，递归自我改进（Recursive Self-Improvement, RSI）仍感觉遥不可及；下一刻，我们已看到其雏形的迹象。

模型能力终于超越大多数人类工程师，长运行智能体（long-running agents）的工具链与基础设施取得进展，数据规模日益庞大，以及将智能体并行化以处理远超任何个人此前所能应对的海量任务、测试和方法的能力，共同造就了一个令人惊叹的飞轮效应。

这一飞轮几乎肯定会以前所未有的速度加速模型进展——或至少以惊人的速度推高前沿技术的天花板。如果你尚未将 RSI 可能带来的结果纳入定价考量，那可能是一个失误。

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: The Changing Physics of Cybersecurity and Drug Development with OpenAI President Greg Brockman
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:19
To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we think that humans should be firmly in the driver's seat, should have control over the future, and this technology should amplify human agency. When I look at the world we're going to be in, where software in some ways is becoming like the barrier to entry, it's becoming so cheap. You don't just want software. Right? You want software that is reliable, that is secure, that you can believe in.

Speaker 1 | 00:19 - 00:32
And so cyber spend, security spend should actually vastly outstrip software spend. I think that people have not yet really internalized how much the physics around cybersecurity are going to change. I think there's to end up with a much more secure world.

Speaker 2 | 00:39 - 01:02
Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, Elad and I talk with Greg Brockman, the cofounder and president of OpenAI. We discuss OpenAI's latest math results, Astra, and why Greg believes AI can now generate genuinely new knowledge. We get into drug discovery dots and his case for why security spending should actually vastly outstrip software spending, which is quite a claim.

Speaker 2 | 01:02 - 01:06
Here's our conversation with Greg Brockmiff. Greg, thanks so much for doing this.

Speaker 1 | 01:06 - 01:08
Thanks, Regina. Thank you for having me.

Speaker 3 | 01:08 - 01:25
So every week in AI feels like a year. And a lot's happened this week for OpenAI. You rolled out GPT-six to over a billion people, which is pretty amazing. There's some really exciting news that you have on the math side. There's all sorts of things that undoubtedly that are happening internally.

Speaker 3 | 01:25 - 01:29
What are you most excited about that's happening right now, both at OpenAI and in the broader AI world? Look, I

Speaker 1 | 01:29 - 02:36
think that in AI, like I have this belief about how OpenAI operates, that there's this cycling quote of it never gets easier, you just go faster, and I think that's very much what happens is that there's just so much activity and that every time you think you're at peak impact and how things are happening, realize that there's actually another level that's possible and it's not just about any one company, it's not just about any one technology, it's really we as a world and society are all coming together to adopt this technology, get the most out of it, to improve everyone's lives. And so I think to me, the math results this week represent a real milestone, right? It's a real moment where if you think about the fundamental driver of human quality of life improving over the past thousand years is technology, right? It's scientific advancement and I think that we now have the ability to massively accelerate scientific discovery and there has always been this question of is AI actually able to come up with new knowledge and at this point, it's just impossible to deny, right? It is definitively, yes, possible.

Speaker 1 | 02:36 - 03:17
Now there is still more to go. I think we not yet coming up with whole, brand new theories, but we are able to resolve these 100 year old math problems and to me, the thing that is very exciting is it is not just about the machine just sort of gives you an answer, right? It's really what can a human equipped with these tools achieve that was unthinkable before and I think it's almost like the leverage of humans to do whatever you want to do, it's going way, way up, right? It's now that you can, if you have a math problem you want go solve, you can solve it, but what about taking that same capability and applying it to biology? What about if you're a small business owner and you want to be able to operate your business well?

Speaker 1 | 03:17 - 03:32
Like that level of intelligence that's tuned for that domain, it's just going to mean that almost this sort of unthinkable results that are aligned with your goals, with your desires, is now going to be within the breach of everyone and that to me is so exciting.

Speaker 3 | 03:32 - 04:07
The RADAR progress has been pretty amazing too because if I look at it, you you used to have problems with arithmetic, right, in early models, I remember people complain, oh, why can't it do basic math? And now you're solving these advanced theorems. As these things continue to advance and starts to really impact areas of math, physics, materials, etcetera, and various applications, there some need if these models get so smart to focus on how to communicate that effectively to people? Or how do you think about the actual communication side of this as you do a very advanced theorem? Because if you look at any field of math, only a very small number of people can ever really adjudicate a theorem that's produced by a person.

Speaker 3 | 04:07 - 04:10
Yes. Right? And so you kind of have this specialization that happens.

Speaker 1 | 04:10 - 05:13
Well, and this, by the way, is something that has always been, like I came from a math background, like I thought I was going to be a mathematician and I was very inspired by mathematicians like Galois or Gauss, right, these people who were working on like a one hundred, four hundred year time horizon, right, and I think there's something deeply beautiful about mathematics being about sort of understanding the structure of the universe and so it's not just about and there's always these questions about is math invented or discovered and that in my mind it's something that the beauty and the meaning of mathematics, it's not something that is objective in some sense, in the eye of the beholder, it's something that appeals to us and there is some amount that's like physical laws and it's about simplicity and, you know, complexity theory and all these things that are maybe more physics but there is something that is also importantly human about it and so to me, it's not just about, I think a lot of the conversation about mathematics, it's not just about here's a proof, no one understands it, great, we resolve the problem.

Speaker 1 | 05:13 - 06:21
It's really about what are the insights that are derived and the thing that I think we will see, but I think that there's promising signs of life on, is that there are beautiful insights within the work that these AIs have done and I think what we're seeing right now is that, you know, we published about almost 400 very important open problems that are now resolved and the mathematical community is going through all of that to look for insights and if you read some of the things that people have posted, domain experts in these particular problems and they say that it's like there is these almost like sort of very surprising ways of applying ideas or incredibly like, wait, why did they use that result over here and that what's coming out is not these incomprehensible theorem or the proofs which, by the way, there is a history of incomprehensible proofs in mathematics. Like, four color theorem is a perfect example of this that is, it's like, okay, we just had the machine check a bunch of cases, like there's no beauty in that. And so I think we're into a different phase of machine discovery.

Speaker 2 | 06:21 - 06:43
I have some optimism that, like, as models also get to better theory of mind, like the ability to figure out, like, what we as humans know and how to get us to follow them on the path to new understanding will also be paved. Right? And and so, like, for example, like, I'm a a math person, but at some point in school, I stopped learning math. And then I did math academy. And then I did, like, chat GPT to help me learn new math.

Speaker 2 | 06:43 - 06:52
